In Kubernetes, readiness probes determine if a container is ready to accept traffic, while liveness probes detect if a container is stuck in a failed state and trigger a restart. Memory limits are enforced by the kernel's OOM (Out-Of-Memory) killer; when a process exceeds its limit, the kernel terminates that specific process rather than restarting the entire container automatically. Consequently, exceeding memory limits causes the application inside the container to crash, which may lead to a restart if a liveness probe fails or if the container is configured to exit on failure, whereas readiness probes only control whether traffic is routed to the pod without affecting its running state.

Readiness probes, liveness probes, and memory limits each affect a Kubernetes pod in different ways. A readiness probe determines if a container is ready to serve traffic; if it fails, the pod is removed from service, meaning traffic is stopped to it. A liveness probe checks if the container is running correctly; if it fails, Kubernetes will restart the container. Memory limits, on the other hand, are resource constraints that, when exceeded, cause the container to be terminated by the container runtime. The component that enforces the memory limit is the container runtime.
